claims.text: A calibrated sub-Tg anneal immediately after melt spinning will improve glass-forming ability.
The same post-melt-spinning anneal will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The proposed treatment is an approximately 10-minute isothermal anneal at Tg minus 20 °C under an inert atmosphere, followed by rapid cooling.
In situ thermal monitoring can keep the treatment below the crystallization threshold.
Free-volume annihilation and internal-stress reduction produce a denser and more uniform atomic arrangement.
Controlled sub-Tg annealing permits localized atomic rearrangements without providing enough energy for crystal nucleation.
The anneal-induced structural state increases kinetic barriers to crystallization.
Increased kinetic barriers to crystallization create a more stable amorphous network.
Annealed samples will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will have lower exothermic crystallization-peak intensity in DSC than as-cast samples.
Post-solidification annealing may increase the critical casting thickness achievable.
The intervention should be effective only when the as-cast sample is fully amorphous.
Deviations in annealing temperature, duration, or atmosphere may cause crystallization or eliminate the benefit.

contradictions.description: The intervention is performed only after an amorphous sample has already formed and is restricted to fully amorphous samples, yet it is claimed to improve glass-forming ability and critical casting thickness. The proposed experiment does not explain how post-solidification treatment can alter the formation or castable thickness of that already-produced sample.
